extracted.intended_audience: congressional staff, policymakers, patent practitioners, industry stakeholders, and other informed readers interested in U.S. Section 101 policy
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and apply U.S. Section 101 standards for patent-eligible subject matter, including judicial exceptions, the Alice/Mayo two-step test, USPTO examiner guidance, and possible legislative responses. Useful for evaluating whether inventions (especially AI/biotech/computer-implemented) meet subject-matter eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-eligible subject matter under Section 101
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 of the Patent Act (35 U.S.C. § 101) sets out four categories of patentable inventions: 'any new and useful [1] process, [2] machine, [3] manufacture, or [4] composition of matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Through Section 101, Congress sought to ensure the patentability of 'anything under the sun that is made by man' that meets all of the other legal requirements for patentability, such as novelty, enablement, and nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicially developed exceptions to Section 101
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court has long held that Section 101 contains implicit exceptions: 'laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas,' when claimed as such, are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three types of nonpatentable discoveries are sometimes called the judicially developed exceptions to patent-eligible subject matter. Historical treatment of these exceptions has varied over time and affects scope of eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step test — Step 1: 'directed to' an ineligible concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step of the Alice/Mayo test addresses whether the patent claims are 'directed to' an ineligible concept (i.e., a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be directed to an ineligible concept, the focus of the claims must be a patent-ineligible concept, as opposed to a technological process. If the patent claims are not directed to an ineligible concept, then the claims are patent eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step test — Step 2: inventive concept requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the second step of the Alice/Mayo test, if the claims are directed to an ineligible concept, then the invention is not patentable unless the patent claims have an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 2 considers the elements of each patent claim, both individually and as an ordered combination, in determining whether they contain additional aspects that 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application of an ineligible concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventionality/Generic-computer implementation cannot supply inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that are conventional, routine, and well understood, such as implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer, cannot supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle means simply reciting conventional technology or routine steps (e.g., using a generic computer) will not transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter; courts evaluate both individual elements and ordered combinations for an inventive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court examples of ineligible claims (illustrative precedents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court invalidated patents as ineligible under Section 101 in several notable cases: a business method for hedging price-fluctuation risk (Bilski v. Kappos, 2010); a method for calibrating drug dosage (Mayo v. Prometheus, 2012); isolated human DNA segments (Ass'n for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics, 2013); and a computer-implemented method of mitigating settlement risk in financial transactions (Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank, 2014).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These decisions illustrate applications of the judicial exceptions and the Alice/Mayo framework and show that certain business methods, natural products, and certain computer-implemented methods have been treated as ineligible, leading to narrower eligibility in software, business methods, and biotechnology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay of Section 101 with other patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 defines the types of inventions that may be patented but is only one statutory gate; eligible subject matter must also meet other legal requirements such as novelty, enablement, and nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claimed invention must satisfy Section 101 and the other statutory requirements—failure on any ground can defeat patentability; policy or legislative changes to Section 101 do not alter these other requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO examiner guidance and its (nonbinding) role
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO issued the 2019 Guidance (incorporated into the MPEP), the 2024 Guidance (providing additional details and AI examples), and a 2025 memo reaffirming the 2024 Guidance to guide patent examiners' application of the Alice/Mayo framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although USPTO guidance is not legally binding in court, it guides examiner practice and appears to have affected allowance rates (e.g., 2019 Guidance generally perceived as lowering Section 101 barriers and increasing allowance rates for AI-related applications relative to the post-Alice period). 2024 Guidance provided specific examples for AI; some stakeholders viewed it as helpful, others wanted more clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization risks for AI inventions under eligibility standards
rubrics_metrics.description: AI inventions may be at risk under the current framework because 'they may be characterized as methods of organizing human activity, mental processes, or mathematical concepts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO analysis showed allowance rates for patent applications containing AI decreased relative to non-AI applications following Alice; the 2024 Guidance aimed to illustrate how eligibility requirements apply to AI inventions but stakeholder views on its sufficiency vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy evaluation criteria for changes to subject-matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders assess subject-matter eligibility reform based on effects on innovation, investment, and industry-specific outcomes; views vary by sector, industry, and firm size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some groups (e.g., civil liberties and nonprofits) support exclusions to prevent monopolies on basic research tools; others (e.g., biotech representatives) warn that restrictive eligibility jeopardizes development of precision medicine, pharmaceuticals, and diagnostics. Policy evaluation should consider differential impacts across economic sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative options for Congress on Section 101
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could (a) abrogate the Alice/Mayo framework and replace it with a closed list of statutorily defined ineligible categories, (b) codify the Alice/Mayo test, (c) replace the framework with a different legal standard, or (d) choose not to pursue legislation and allow courts and USPTO guidance to continue to develop the doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed legislative approaches vary in scope and specificity (e.g., narrow exceptions for inventions existing solely in the human mind or independently of human activity, or broader lists including mathematical formulas, purely mental processes, substantially economic/cultural processes, purely natural processes, unmodified natural material). Congress must consider how the scope/specificity of statutory exceptions would impact eligible inventions.
